MEPS data on medical expenses are collected from both household respondents in the Household Component and from a sample of their health care providers in the Medical Provider Component. Expense data are collected at the event level for each medical event type and a weighted hot-deck procedure is used for imputation.

# Neural model forecasts medical event counts and ranks spending better than two GLMs in US survey data, preprint finds

A preprint by Eva Flonner proposes a neural model, built on a causal Transformer, that follows each person's health claims over time, including reporting delays and medical cost inflation. Fitted on US household survey records of medical events and spending from all payers for 2019-2021 and tested on 2022, it forecast event counts and ranked spending better than two generalised linear models. It is not peer reviewed and was not tested on insurer claims.

Source checkedRead against arXiv,

In context: this report covers a source published on 16 Nov 2026.

A preprint posted on arXiv on 16 November 2026 by Eva Flonner asks whether a more flexible neural model of each person's claim history predicts health insurance claims better than conventional actuarial benchmarks. It has not been peer reviewed. The model, a neural marked point process, uses a causal Transformer to read past claims and estimate the chance of each claim type occurring next, together with claim size, reporting delay and medical cost inflation. One claim can raise the chance of further claims, and claim types can affect each other.

The author tests it twice. First on simulated data: 10,000 synthetic contracts over six years from January 2021, with inpatient, outpatient, dental and pharmacy claims, giving 316,620 reported and 3,791 unreported claims. The model was fitted on 2019 to 2021 and asked to forecast 2022.

Health insurance claims exhibit temporal dependence, as previous claims may provide information about the timing, type and amount of subsequent claims. Such dependencies are difficult to capture with traditional actuarial models based on aggregated claim counts. We investigate a neural marked point process in which a causal Transformer represents individual claim histories and determines type-specific conditional intensities, allowing for self-excitation and interactions between claim types. Patients who suffer from chronic conditions or diseases are susceptible to experiencing repeated events of the same type (e.g. seizures), termed ‘recurrent events’. Prediction models can be used to predict the risk of recurrence so that intervention or management can be tailored accordingly, but statistical methodology can vary. The objective of this systematic review was to identify and describe statistical approaches that have been applied for the development and validation of multivariable prediction models with recurrent event data. jina.snippet:
Thomas N. Nipen Ivar A. Seierstad Affiliation:Norwegian Meteorological Institute, Box 43 Blindern, Oslo, Norway.

###### Abstract

During the last two years, tremendous progress in global data-driven weather models trained on numerical weather prediction (NWP) re-analysis data has been made. The most recent models trained on the ERA5 at 0.25° resolution demonstrate forecast quality on par with ECMWF’s high-resolution model with respect to a wide selection of verification metrics. In this study, one of these models, the Pangu-Weather, is compared to several NWP models with and without probabilistic post-processing for 2-meter temperature and 10-meter wind speed forecasting at 183 Norwegian SYNOP stations up to +60 hours ahead. The NWP models included are the ECMWF HRES, ECMWF ENS and the Harmonie-AROME ensemble model MEPS with 2.5 km spatial resolution. Results show that the performances of the global models are on the same level with Pangu-Weather being slightly better than the ECMWF models for temperature and slightly worse for wind speed. The MEPS model clearly provided the best forecasts for both parameters. The post-processing improved the forecast quality considerably for all models, but to a larger extent for the coarse-resolution global models due to stronger systematic deficiencies in these. Apart from this, the main characteristics in the scores were more or less the same with and without post-processing. keenable.title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
keenable.snippet: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5∘ resolution and lead times of 2–10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979–2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Revisiting deterministic forecasts for 2020, we find that model rankings can reverse when only the verification reference changes, so that the choice of reference is itself part of the result. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time.

keenable.title: Regression Models Meet Foundation Models: A Hybrid-AI Approach to Practical Electricity Price Forecasting
keenable.snippet: non-stationarity, making accurate forecasting a significant challenge. While cutting-edge time series foundation models (TSFMs) effectively capture temporal dependencies, they typically underutilize cross-variate correlations and non-periodic patterns that are essential for price forecasting. #### 3.5 Using MEPS Data for Trend Analysis  
For analysts using the MEPS data for trend analysis, there are uncertainties associated with 2020, 2021, and 2022 data quality, as discussed in Section C.3.1. Evaluations of important MEPS estimates suggest that the estimates are of reasonable quality. Nevertheless, analysts are advised to exercise caution when interpreting these estimates, particularly for trend analyses, because the pandemic substantially affected healthcare access and related factors (e.g., health insurance coverage, employment status).  
MEPS began in 1996, and the utility of the survey for analyzing healthcare trends expands with each additional year of data; however, when examining trends over time using MEPS, the duration being analyzed should be considered. In particular, large shifts in survey estimates over short periods (e.g., from one year to the next) that are statistically significant should be interpreted with caution, unless they are attributable to known factors such as changes in public policy, economic conditions, or the MEPS methodology.

Background: Discrete-time event history analysis (EHA) is the standard approach taken when modelling fertility histories collected in surveys, where the date of birth is often recorded imprecisely. This method is commonly used to investigate the factors associated with the time to a first or subsequent conception or birth. Although there is an emerging trend towards the smooth incorporation of continuous covariates in the broader literature, this is yet to be formally embraced in the context of birth events. Methods: We fit parity-specific logistic GAMs to data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, learning about the effects of age, period, time since last birth, educational qualification, and country of birth. First, we select the most parsimonious GAMs that fit the data sufficiently well. Then we compare them with corresponding models that use the existing methods of categorical, polynomial, and piecewise linear spline representations in terms of fit, complexity, and substantive insights gained. Results: We find that smooth terms can offer considerable improvements in precision and efficiency, particularly for highly non-linear effects and interactions between continuous variables. Their flexibility enables the detection of important features that are missed or estimated imprecisely by comparator methods. Frailty refers to unobserved, random effects that account for differences in survival rates among individuals that cannot be explained solely by measured covariates, while MSMs extend survival models to allow transitions between multiple states over time. This joint application help in understanding not just whether an event will happen, but when and how individuals move between various health states before reaching a terminal state.

Frailty models were initially proposed by Vaupel et al. to explain unobserved heterogeneity in survival times across ostensibly similar individuals. These models frequently extend the Cox proportional hazards (Cox PH) model, which is among the most prevalent models utilised for comparing treatments in survival analysis. However, while the Cox PH model posits that the hazard function can be fully characterized by the baseline hazard and covariate values, it does not account for the unobserved variability or random effects. This is where frailty models are particularly useful. Frailty introduces random effects that adjust for unobserved heterogeneity between individuals or clusters. The Markov assumption in multistate models, which posits that future states depend only on the current state and not on prior transitions, often fails when unobserved effects are not accounted for.

In multistate models, individuals transition through various states (e.g., from healthy to diseased to dead), making them ideal for analyzing chronic diseases that involve multiple stages. Incorporating frailty into MSMs addresses the association between the transition intensities of individuals, as the likelihood of transitioning from one state to another is not independent but often influenced by underlying, unmeasured factors.

Title: JudgeCast: Time Series Forecasting with Experience-Informed Covariate Judgements

Authors: Donguk Kwon, Wooseok Jeong, Dongha Lee

Abstract: Covariate effects vary across contexts and shift over time, requiring forecasters to assess how to use them for each forecasting context. As forecasting proceeds, observations for earlier forecasts become available, providing feedback on past covariate use for subsequent forecasts. However, when multiple covariates act together, the forecast error reveals the numerical discrepancy from the observation but not how the covariates should have been used. We introduce JudgeCast, an experience-based framework for time series forecasting with covariates. Following the judgmental adjustment practice, a frozen TSFM provides the base forecast, while a frozen LLM uses the current context and relevant experience to adjust it. Within the adjustment, assessing covariate effects and determining the numerical adjustment serve distinct roles, so JudgeCast first forms explicit covariate-wise judgments and then determines the adjustment. After observation, JudgeCast uses the observed residual of the base forecast to reconstruct alternative judgments and evaluates the original and alternatives through their resulting adjustments. The best-performing decision is selected and retained as validated experience for subsequent forecasts. Across diverse real-world datasets, JudgeCast outperforms strong baselines. Ablations show that explicit covariate-wise judgment can improve forecast-time adjustment, while residual-guided experience construction yields more reliable forecasting gains than retaining raw decisions as experience.

seltz.snippet:
How much history should a time-series transformer see for a one-hour-ahead forecast? An hourly series can carry two kinds of evidence at once. Last week’s value at the same hour may explain a repeating load cycle. The last three observations may show that a machine has just changed state. A short history can see the change but miss the earlier cycle; a long history can contain both, yet may spend most of its capacity on irrelevant or obsolete observations. **The useful context length is the shortest history that improves the decision you actually make, on forecast origins the competing lengths can all serve, at an acceptable cost.** It is an empirical choice, not a property of the transformer alone.

This guide sets up that comparison. Its running example is a *hypothetical* hourly load series with daily and weekly patterns and occasional abrupt jumps. The dates and readings in that worked example are synthetic; a separate measured-data check appears below. The same logic applies to other multivariate sequences, provided the prediction time, target, and meaning of a step are made explicit.

## Define what one prediction is allowed to know

Suppose a forecasting service runs after hour `t` has closed. It receives measured load `y_t`, temperature, operating mode, and other observations available by that time, then predicts load for hour `t+1`. A context of `L` rows contains positions `t-L+1` through `t`; the target is `y_{t+1}`. One step means one hour only if the data have been put on a regular hourly grid. If sensors report irregularly, 168 events need not represent a week. Resample with an explicit missing-data policy, or make elapsed time and gaps part of the representation.

seltz.snippet:
A person is employed at age 30 and holds a degree. For a model estimating their risk of a sustained unemployment spell over the next two years, how much earlier history should count? The last job might be enough. Or a return to work after a recent spell may matter in a way that a snapshot misses. Ten years of records might add information, but they also add observation gaps, changes in coding, and people whose histories are shorter for reasons related to the outcome.

**Choose the context window against a defined life-course question, then test its incremental value against a strong static-history baseline at the same prediction landmarks.** A longer event sequence is useful only if it changes a measured decision or improves a relevant estimate on data that were genuinely unavailable during model development. seltz.title: sistemalabs | Does Historical Streamflow Improve River Discharge Forecasts?
seltz.snippet:
Equal river flows can hide different histories. A gauge reads 10 cubic metres per second at noon. Yesterday it reached 10 on the way up; today it reached 10 on the way down. Should the next six-hour forecast be the same? A model that sees only the current reading has to give the same answer if all its other inputs are identical. A model that sees the preceding rainfall, upstream flow, and shape of the hydrograph can give different answers. Whether the second answer is *better* is an empirical question.

Historical streamflow can improve a discharge forecast when the current reading hides information about the recent rise, recession, or antecedent conditions. It is useful in a particular basin only if that extra history improves held-out forecasts beyond simpler lag, slope, and rainfall-aware baselines. That question matters when an evaluation rewards average accuracy across all hours but hides errors around event onset and recession. It also matters for the interpretation of a learned representation: two observations with the same endpoint may encode different recent forcing and different possible future responses. The useful test is not whether a sequence model draws different embeddings for those observations. It is whether the extra history improves a defined downstream prediction on genuinely comparable forecast origins.

This guide sets out such a test for environmental sequence ML engineers. It uses discharge as the observable endpoint and short-horizon discharge forecasting as the primary task. Soil moisture, groundwater, upstream measurements, and ecological sensors can be added when they are available at the forecast issue time, but they are different measurements with different coverage and quality. They should not be assumed to exist merely because the model accepts multiple columns.

The M competitions are a series of large, open forecasting contests, run by Spyros Makridakis since 1982, that test which methods actually predict the future best. No single forecasting model wins everywhere. The right choice comes from reading your series' pattern, its trend, its seasonality and its autocorrelation, then shortlisting the models that fit that pattern and backtesting them against a simple baseline so the data, not the hype, picks the winner. This guide walks that process end to end in R, using base R plus the forecast package.

Code examples run against R 4.6.0

ultimate.snippet:
We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), a general event-aware forecasting framework built on a shared Event Response Function (ERF). The ERF models event effects according to event type and relative temporal position and is shared across the historical and forecast windows. Loki lifts out estimated event-induced deviations from historical observations before forecasting, then uses the same ERF to kick in responses to known future events. This formulation separates event-response modeling from temporal forecasting while coupling historical attribution and future generation through a shared mechanism. Across five forecasting benchmarks, Loki achieves the best standardized MAE on all five datasets, reducing error by approximately 2.2%–11.7% over the strongest non-Loki baseline.

We propose Loki (Lift Out, Kick In), an event-aware forecasting framework built around a shared Event Response Function (ERF). We focus on intermittently occurring, time-bounded events whose schedules are known across the historical and forecast windows. Their effects may extend beyond the event intervals themselves. As illustrated in Figure 1(b), Loki first lifts out estimated event-related variation from historical observations, allowing a forecasting backbone to predict the adjusted trajectory, and then kicks in the response associated with known future events. Using the same ERF for both operations allows their learning signals to jointly constrain a common response model through the forecasting objective.

ultimate.title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
ultimate.snippet: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5∘ resolution and lead times of 2–10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979–2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Revisiting deterministic forecasts for 2020, we find that model rankings can reverse when only the verification reference changes, so that the choice of reference is itself part of the result. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time.

While cutting-edge time series foundation models (TSFMs) effectively capture temporal dependencies, they typically underutilize cross-variate correlations and non-periodic patterns that are essential for price forecasting. Conversely, regression models excel at capturing feature interactions but are limited to future-available inputs, ignoring crucial historical drivers that are unavailable at forecast time. We instantiate this paradigm into a lightweight, plug-and-play framework for electricity price forecasting. A forecasting model can be estimated correctly and still be evaluated incorrectly. The central design question is whether each forecast uses only information that would actually have been available when it was made. A random split of a time series can put later observations into the training sample for a forecast of an earlier period; the resulting evaluation then benefits from information unavailable in real use.

A rolling-origin evaluation avoids that particular problem by moving the forecast origin forward through time. At each origin, the model is fitted or updated using an explicitly defined history, and its forecast is recorded for a future target.
